Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027: Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline

November 12, 2026

Kyle Koppe

BLOG

5 min.

Have you been wondering what the prevailing cloud security best practices for 2027 might be? Unlike years past, 2027 is set to center around the data-to-AI pipeline. Data platforms, AI services and autonomous agents now run side by side across multiple clouds and the data moving between them carries the most business value and the biggest security risk. Organizations planning their 2027 security programs need practices that protect that entire movement, not just the environments on either end.

TL;DR – A critical cloud security best practice for 2027 is going to center around securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system, with protection and access policies following data from collection through model training, deployment and agentic AI use.

Key takeaways:

Own the configuration. Under the shared responsibility model, organizations are responsible for securing the AI and data services they use and default settings need tuning to each environment.

Enforce through architecture. Policy-as-code, infrastructure-as-code and automated guardrails turn security strategy into controls that hold up at scale.

Start with a baseline and build from there. Assess, plan and engineer pipeline security as a holistic motion, starting from wherever you are and building toward a scalable architecture that’s ready for what comes next.

Six Cloud Security Best Practices for 2027

Data teams and AI teams often work on different platforms with different priorities. Similarly, security programs have traditionally treated data security and AI security as separate disciplines. Moving into the coming year, organizations that secure the pipeline end-to-end will allow protection and access policies to carry forward as information moves between environments. This strategy allows them to enable new AI workloads to come online quickly without sacrificing security.

By following six interconnected practices, organizations can strengthen each individual layer of the cloud environment and then connect them into a cohesive, policy-driven foundation.

1. Treat Shared Responsibility as an AI Practice

Under the cloud shared responsibility model, the customer owns the security configuration of services such as Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker and Google Gemini Enterprise (Vertex AI). These services ship with default settings designed for broad use. Organizations should review and tune access controls, content filtering and model permissions to match their own data, risk tolerance and compliance obligations.

2. Classify Data Before AI Consumes It

Sensitive data discovery and classification work best when they happen early. Data security posture management (DSPM) gives teams visibility into where sensitive information lives, who can reach it and how it moves, so they can apply protection before data reaches a model or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application.

3. Enforce Policy as Code

Documented policies only reduce risk when they are enforced. Policy-as-code and infrastructure-as-code let teams define security requirements once and apply them consistently across every environment, pipeline and deployment, which keeps controls aligned as cloud footprints grow.

4. Govern Every Identity, Human and Non-Human

AI workloads and agents act as identities in the cloud and they can accumulate permissions quickly. Mapping entitlements, enforcing least privilege and reviewing privileged access for data and AI administrators help limit the reach of any single account or agent.

5. Build Compliance Into the Architecture

AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and the CSA AI Controls Matrix sit alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS. Aligning architecture to these frameworks from the start creates audit-ready governance and reduces rework as new regulations take effect.

6. Secure the Data-to-AI Pipeline as One System

This is the practice the others point toward. Before data reaches a model or agent, teams copy, combine and transform it across databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines. At each stage, organizations need to preserve data integrity, understand sensitivity and origin and limit access to sensitive information.

Translate Strategy into Action with GuidePoint Security’s Secure Cloud Platform for Data and AI

GuidePoint Security’s new Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI bring together assessments, platform advisory and cloud engineering to secure the full pipeline, from collection and preparation through architecture, development, deployment and secure agentic and generative AI use. GuidePoint cloud experts translate governance requirements into enforceable controls such as encryption, access policies, content filtering and model access restrictions.

Data Services: Build AI-ready data platforms on a Medallion Architecture (Bronze, Silver and Gold layers), with DSPM, sensitive data discovery, classification and platform policy configuration built into each layer.

AI Services: Strengthen AI platform configuration, machine learning operations (MLOps) pipeline integrity and policy enforcement across native AI solution and third-party AI SaaS platforms.

Every engagement scales to the organization’s maturity, risk posture and AI roadmap:

Health Check: Baseline security posture across platform configurations, data exposure and AI operational readiness so remediation starts with what matters most.

Advisory: Align security investments with regulatory and business requirements through data protection strategies, governance frameworks and roadmaps.

Engineering: Turn strategy into production infrastructure with secure databases, automated pipelines, policy-as-code enforcement and infrastructure-as-code foundations designed to scale with continued AI innovation.

GuidePoint Security brings vendor-objective, hands-on experience across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and major SaaS ecosystems, including native tools such as Microsoft Purview, Amazon Macie, Google Cloud DLP and Oracle Data Safe. Engagements also connect with complementary GuidePoint services, including Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC), Application Security, Identity and Access Management and threat simulation.

Get Started

Check out our Secure Cloud Platform for Data and AI datasheet. Then, schedule a Secure Cloud Platform Health Check to establish a clear view of data platform configuration, pipeline security and AI readiness and to identify where to focus first in 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the top cloud security best practices for 2027?

Key cloud security best practices for 2027 include owning the security configuration of cloud AI services, classifying data before AI consumes it, enforcing policy as code, governing human and non-human identities, building compliance into the architecture and securing the full data-to-AI pipeline as one connected system.

What is the data-to-AI pipeline?

The data-to-AI pipeline is the path data takes from collection and preparation through storage, transformation, model training, deployment and use by generative and agentic AI applications. It typically spans databases, storage systems, SaaS platforms and processing pipelines across multiple clouds.

Why is securing the data-to-AI pipeline a cloud security best practice?

AI models and agents are only as trustworthy as the data they rely on. Securing the pipeline end to end preserves data integrity, tracks sensitivity and origin and keeps access policies in place as data moves between environments and new AI workloads are introduced.

Who is responsible for securing cloud AI services like Copilot, Bedrock and Vertex AI?

The customer is. Cloud providers secure the underlying infrastructure, but the customer owns configuration, access controls, content filtering and model permissions for AI services. Default settings are designed for broad use, not your risk profile.

What is policy-as-code?

Policy-as-code is the practice of writing security rules as machine-readable code that deploys automatically with infrastructure. It eliminates manual configuration and ensures every environment gets the same controls from day one.

What is DSPM and how does it support AI security?

DSPM continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud environments. For AI security, it identifies which data AI models can access, flags overexposed training sets and tracks data lineage from source to model.

Which AI regulations and frameworks should cloud security programs plan for in 2027?

Organizations should plan for AI-specific frameworks such as the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, the CSA AI Controls Matrix and state AI legislation, alongside established requirements such as GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS.

What are GuidePoint Security's Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI?

Secure Cloud Platform Services for Data and AI are GuidePoint Security services that combine health checks, advisory and engineering to secure the full data-to-AI pipeline across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and major SaaS platforms.

Where should an organization start with Secure Cloud Platform Services?

Most organizations start with a Secure Cloud Platform Health Check to baseline platform configuration, data exposure and AI readiness. They can then add advisory or engineering services as their programs mature.

CMMC: Understanding the Difference Between a POA&M and an OPA

November 10, 2026

Jason Spencer

BLOG

5 min.

Understanding the difference between a Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) and an Operational Plan of Action (OPA) starts with recognizing that these two documents serve different purposes under 32 CFR Part 170 (the CMMC Program).

TL;DR – LA Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) and an Operational Plan of Action (OPA) serve fundamentally different purposes under CMMC and confusing the two is one of the fastest ways to stall your certification.

A POA&M is tied to a C3PAO assessment finding, carries a 180-day closure deadline and directly impacts certification

An OPA tracks temporary vulnerabilities found during normal operations with no fixed timeline or certification consequence

Most compliance failures come from documentation mistakes, not security gaps

The Key Attributes of a POA&M and OPA

A POA&M is a formal remediation plan created in response to a C3PAO assessment finding where a security requirement is marked “Not Met”. It carries a strict 180-day closure deadline and directly impacts CMMC certification. An OPA, by contrast, tracks temporary vulnerabilities discovered during normal operations and carries no fixed deadline or certification consequence.

The following table provides a side-by-side comparison of the key attributes that distinguish these two documents.

Attribute

POA&M (Plan of Action & Milestones)

OPA (Operational Plan of Action)

Purpose

Documents NOT MET security requirements found during a CMMC assessment; tracks remediation to full compliance

Documents ongoing operational security activities, continuous improvement and risk management

Time-Bound

Yes — strict 180-day remediation deadline

No — ongoing with no fixed deadline

Trigger

Created when a practice is scored NOT MET during a C3PAO assessment

Created proactively as part of ongoing security operations

Certification Impact

Allows conditional CMMC Level 2 certification

Cannot cover or paper over a NOT MET requirement

Eligible Practices

Only 1-point practices (up to 22 maximum)

Applies broadly to operational improvements and enhancements

Score Threshold

Must score 80% or higher (88/110 practices MET)

No scoring threshold — exists independently of assessment

Close-Out

Formal close-out assessment by C3PAO within 180 days

Reviewed and updated as part of continuous monitoring; no formal close-out

Failure Consequence

Loses conditional certification if not remediated within 180 days

No direct certification consequence; may become findings in future assessments

Nature

Reactive — addresses deficiencies found during assessment

Proactive — addresses planned improvements and ongoing risk management

What Must a POA&M and an OPA Include to Pass a CMMC Assessment?

Knowing the difference between a POA&M and an OPA is only the first step. Organizations must also understand what each document needs to contain to satisfy assessor expectations and regulatory requirements. A strong POA&M goes beyond acknowledging a gap. It must include defined remediation steps, responsible parties, resource and budget requirements, milestones with specific dates and a firm 180-day closure commitment. A strong OPA must clearly identify the temporary vulnerability, describe the mitigation or correction plan, outline the current risk posture and explain the monitoring approach.

The table below breaks down the required content elements for each document type.

Strong POA&M Must Include

Strong OPA Must Include

Clear explanation of what is missing and why

Defined remediation steps with responsible parties

Resource requirements and budget implications

Milestones with specific completion dates

Evidence of active progress toward closure

180-day closure deadline commitment

Identification of the temporary vulnerability or deficiency

Explanation of how it will be mitigated, corrected or eliminated

Current risk posture description

Monitoring and tracking approach

No fixed deadline required - duration depends on circumstances

8 of the Most Common POA&M and OPA Mistakes Under CMMC

Even organizations with mature security programs frequently stumble when preparing POA&Ms and OPAs for CMMC compliance. These mistakes range from treating routine vulnerabilities as OPA items (when standard vulnerability management processes under RA.L2-3.11.3 and SI.L1-3.14.1 should apply) to submitting vague timelines that assessors will immediately flag. Other common errors include omitting required mitigation details from OPAs, resubmitting pre-CMMC implementation plans as POA&Ms, assuming compliance without completing a gap assessment or collecting actual evidence, making CUI scoping errors, practices not eligible for the POA&M and preparing for the wrong assessment criteria entirely.

The table below outlines eight of the most frequent mistakes and explains why each one matters.

#

Mistake

Why It Matters

1

Treating routine vulnerabilities as OPA items

Not every vulnerability warrants an OPA. Use standard vulnerability management (RA.L2-3.11.3 / SI.L1-3.14.1) instead.

2

Using vague timelines in POA&Ms

Assessors expect specific dates, resources and checkpoints - not general language.

3

Leaving mitigation details out of the OPA

CA.L2-3.12.2 requires documenting how deficiencies will be mitigated, corrected or eliminated.

4

Resubmitting the NIST SP 800-171 implementation POA&M

A pre-CMMC project plan is not a POA&M for assessment findings; these are distinct documents.

5

Assumed compliance without evidence

Organizations often assume compliance without completing a gap assessment or actual evidence collection.

6

CUI scoping errors

Organizations fail to understand FCI and/or CUI contracts and flows in their environment.

7

Preparing for the wrong assessment criteria

Failing to identify FCI for Level 1 or CUI for Level 2 compliance.

8

Practices not eligible for POA&M inclusion

Not POA&M eligible practices and objectives will lead to failure self-assessment and C3PAO assessment.

How Can Organizations Avoid POA&M and OPA Failures During CMMC Certification?

Knowing what belongs in a POA&M versus an OPA is the first step. Building them with the specificity, evidence and structure that will hold up under a C3PAO assessment is the harder one. GuidePoint Security CMMC Readiness Assessment and Advisory Services can help your organizations at every stage of the CMMC journey, from scoping and gap assessments through documentation, remediation and assessment readiness. Organizations that go through the process walk into their assessment with clean documentation, defensible evidence and a clear understanding of where they stand.

FAQs

What happens if a POA&M is not closed within 180 days?

The organization loses its conditional CMMC certification status. The C3PAO must verify closure before final certification is granted. There is no extension process.

When should an organization use an OPA instead of standard vulnerability management?

An OPA applies when a temporary deficiency falls outside routine patching or scanning cycles. Standard vulnerability management under RA.L2-3.11.3 handles known, recurring issues. Use an OPA for gaps that need a documented mitigation plan.

Why do organizations fail POA&M reviews during CMMC assessments?

Most failures stem from documentation gaps, not security gaps. Organizations submit vague timelines, omit mitigation details or reuse pre-CMMC implementation plans. Assessors expect specific dates, responsible parties and evidence of progress.

Do subcontractors need their own POA&M for CMMC?

Yes. Each organization seeking CMMC certification must maintain its own POA&M. Subcontractors cannot rely on a prime contractor’s documentation.

What happens if a vulnerability is found after a CMMC assessment?

Post-assessment vulnerabilities are tracked through an OPA, not a POA&M. The OPA documents the issue and mitigation plan without triggering a new assessment cycle.

Who Checked the AI Agent’s ID at the Front Door?

November 9, 2026

Kevin Converse

BLOG

5 min.

I’ve worked with several security teams who were confident they knew how many agents were running in their environment. That confidence didn’t survive the assessment. What we uncovered were hundreds of agents operating on inherited authority, cached credentials, shared service accounts and user sessions that were never designed to be reused by autonomous systems. No one had authorized them. No one owned them. And no one knew the full scope of what they could do.

TL;DR – The cybersecurity industry is treating AI agent security as a permissions problem. It’s a delegation problem. The organizations scaling AI with confidence are the ones building trust chains now, not waiting for the standards to arrive.

Delegation, not permissions, is the gap. Agents don’t just access resources. They inherit authority no one explicitly granted.

Adoption is outpacing governance: most organizations can deploy agents fast, but few have lifecycle controls to match.

The first move is a registry, not a product: identify every agent, assign a human sponsor and define its purpose before buying anything.

Why AI Agent Security Is a Delegation Problem

The cybersecurity industry has spent the last year asking the wrong question about AI agents. Most have been focused on what agents can access, what permissions they hold and how to revoke them. Those are valid concerns, but they only scratch the surface. The deeper question is about delegation: who authorized this agent to act, on whose behalf, under what conditions and what happens when the chain of trust breaks.

Every Agent Represents a Trust Chain

When an employee delegates a task to an AI agent, a chain of trust forms.

The employee trusts the agent to act within certain boundaries

The organization trusts the employee to delegate responsibility

The systems the agent touches trust the credentials the agent presents

Each link in that chain carries an assumption about what the agent is authorized to do and in most organizations today, none of those assumptions have been formally defined.

This is what separates agentic AI from every previous identity challenge. Cloud identities, service accounts and workload identities all involve access. Agents involve authority. An agent doesn’t need permission to read a database; it needs authority to decide what to do with what it reads and then execute that decision across multiple systems before a human reviews the output.

This should raise major red flags for security experts. Privileged access management, role-based access control and service account governance all involve some form of delegated authority. For AI agents, that delegation is happening dynamically, at machine speed and without human knowledge that authority has been extended at all.

Six Problems Security Leaders Are Reporting

In the study Managing Agentic AI Through the Identity Control Plane: What Organizations Should Look For, conducted by IDC and sponsored by GuidePoint Security, panelists across industries described six interconnected problems in their own words:

Problem 1: “I cannot see or count my agents”

Problem 2: “Agents are breaking my identity tooling”

Problem 3: “Privilege is sprawling at machine speed”

Problem 4: “I can no longer trust the human signal”

Problem 5: “Governance and ownership are lagging adoption”

Problem 6: “There is a risk I do not control”

These remarks reveal something important about the nature of the risk. Identity tooling built for human lifecycles, where HR provides the join and leave signals, doesn’t apply to entities that never walk out the door. And when AI-generated impersonation can fake the human approval that the entire sponsor model depends on, the trust architecture has a gap before it even starts.

Why Maturity Assessments Miss the Real Gap

44% of organizations rank non-human identity and AI agent security as their top IAM priority over the next 12 to 24 months. But priority and readiness are not the same thing.

Across these six problems, the panel converged on one consensus: every agent needs a named human sponsor and managed lifecycle. That lifecycle includes gated intake, an approved purpose, scoped access, expiration and recertification and a clean revocation path.

However, adoption is outpacing governance and internally many organizations are struggling to communicate the issue. Managers closer to the problem report bigger gaps than directors, VPs and C-suite. The implication in this is that maturity decisions about where to invest and what to prioritize need to be informed by practitioners who have their hands on keyboards, not shaped exclusively by leadership’s more optimistic view.

What Organizations Can Do to Address the Gap

No single vendor is covering every part of the governance gap. The market is maturing quickly, but the best choice today is the one that closes the highest-priority gaps and can be operationally sustained by the team. Three steps to start:

1. Build an Authoritative Inventory

Not a one-time discovery sweep, but a registry. Every agent in the environment needs to be identified, bound to a named owner and assessed against a defined purpose.

2. Separate the Registry Decision From the Runtime Decision

Knowing who the agent is, its sponsor, its purpose and what it is allowed to touch can start now. How each agent proves its identity cryptographically at runtime, where emerging standards for workload identity such as SPIFFE and SPIRE are still maturing, is a decision that can wait for the market to settle.

3. Align Controls With Emerging Frameworks

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), the EU AI Act and the OWASP Non-Human Identity Top 10 all provide structure for building governance around this new identity class. Prioritize the agents with the most critical access first.

Start With Discovery, Not Standards

The industry will build the standards, protocols and tooling to manage delegation at machine speed. What it will not do is go back and redesign the trust chains that were never built in the first place. The organizations that start now, with discovery, ownership and lifecycle governance, will be the ones that scale AI with confidence.

We meet your organization wherever you are on the maturity curve with a vendor-objective approach, supporting your team in matching programs to your environment and risk profile.

FAQs

What happens when an AI agent's trust chain breaks?

The agent continues operating with authority no one is monitoring. Without a revocation path tied to a human sponsor, compromised agents can move laterally across systems undetected.

How is AI agent delegation different from service account access?

Service accounts authenticate to a single system with static credentials. AI agents inherit authority from a human sponsor and make autonomous decisions across multiple systems at machine speed.

What risks do organizations face without an AI agent registry?

Unregistered agents accumulate privileges no one audits. When a breach occurs, security teams cannot scope the blast radius because they have no inventory of what agents exist or what they can reach.

Who should own AI agent governance inside an organization?

Identity and security teams share responsibility, but every agent needs a named human sponsor accountable for its purpose, scope and lifecycle. Without clear ownership, governance gaps compound as agent counts grow.

How do SPIFFE and SPIRE apply to AI agent identity?

SPIFFE provides a standard for issuing cryptographic identities to workloads and SPIRE is its runtime implementation. These standards are still maturing but will eventually let agents prove identity at runtime without shared credentials.

Post-Quantum Cryptography Part 2: 2030 Is Not the Deadline

November 5, 2026

Timothy Amerson

BLOG

5 min.

TL;DR – GAO’s latest report shows why waiting for the compliance deadline could mean arriving years too late.

In Part 1, Post-Quantum Cryptography: Migrate by Risk, Not by Checkbox, I argued that post-quantum cryptography (PQC) cannot be treated as a compliance exercise. The Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) October 2026 report, GAO-27-108740, shows why: none of the 24 Chief Financial Officers (CFO) Act agencies fully addressed cryptographic inventory, funding assessment or testing and not one had tested PQC.

The audit ran February 2024 through September 2025, before Executive Order (EO) 14412 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Memorandum M-26-15 accelerated the migration – so this is the baseline the Federal Government carried into the accelerated period. In GAO’s words, the gaps “increase the risk that their transitions to quantum-resistant cryptography will occur too late.” That makes the real deadline much closer than 2030.

GAO Put Numbers Behind the Problem

In Part 1, I wrote that when an organization cannot see its cryptography, the inventory gap is not a footnote – it is the program. GAO’s report, Quantum Computing: Federal Actions Needed to Prepare for Emerging Cyber Threat, puts numbers behind that point: only one of 24 agencies fully addressed the prioritized-inventory activities, 18 reported lacking cryptography expertise with no plan to close the gap, 23 had no documented inventory maintenance process, none fully addressed funding and none had tested PQC in their environment.

Figure 1. How the 24 CFO Act agencies scored against GAO's three preparatory practices. Source: GAO-27-108740.

These are not simply compliance findings. They are indicators of execution risk. If I cannot see quantum-vulnerable cryptography, I cannot prioritize it; if I cannot prioritize it, I cannot budget it; if I have not tested the replacement, I do not know what will break.

What Did Waiting Look Like?

The part of the report I keep rereading is not the scorecard. It is the explanations agencies gave, in good faith, for why each practice could wait a little longer: too early for automated tools or waiting on the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to name them (CISA says it never asked anyone to wait); too early to test (open-source PQC tooling has existed for years); too early to document funding without vendor pricing – which is how the Government arrived at an approximate $7.1 billion estimate OMB itself calls a rough order of magnitude.

Figure 2. The reasons agencies gave GAO for deferring action and GAO's response to each. Source: GAO-27-108740, pp. 26-33.

None of these reasons is unreasonable on its own. Together they form a dependency chain: no automation, so no inventory; no inventory, so no funding estimate; no testing, so no idea what breaks. Every year spent waiting for a better tool or a vendor quote is a year subtracted from the migration clock – the one clock agencies actually control.

Waiting for certainty is a decision. It just is not a documented one.

2030 Is a Compliance Line, Not a Risk Line

One concern I continue to have is that the December 31, 2030 deadline creates a false sense of time.

Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks, requires Federal High Value Assets (HVAs) and high-impact systems to use PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030 and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. OMB Memorandum M-26-15, Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography, implements that direction for civilian agencies in five phases, from discovery in 2026-2027 through full migration by 2035 – and frames 2030 as mitigating as much quantum risk as feasible by that date, not starting then. EO 14306 adds Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 by January 2, 2030.

The nearest milestones have already arrived: a named PQC migration lead within 30 days of EO 14412 and a PQC Migration Plan to OMB and the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD) within 120 days of the June 24, 2026 memorandum.

That date is October 22, 2026. The planning clock is not approaching. It is already running.

Figure 3. The three PQC clocks: the compliance clock set by policy, the migration clock each agency controls and the data confidentiality clock that neither policy nor the agency can reset.

But Even October 22 Is Not the Real Security Deadline

Compliance gives us dates. Risk gives us a different clock. The question is not when will a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) arrive, but how long does our information need to remain protected?

An adversary does not need a CRQC today to create a future compromise. They only need to collect the encrypted data today. That is the harvest-now, decrypt-later problem; EO 14412 names it in its first paragraph and GAO makes it concrete, citing collection techniques already in use, from Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) rerouting to supply-chain compromise. Two further GAO points belong in every briefing:

Detection will not save you. Using a CRQC to derive a private key from a public key “is not an event that can be detected by the victim organization’s cybersecurity tools.”

The exposure is in transit and in key establishment. Data at rest is generally protected by symmetric cryptography, which is not currently projected to be vulnerable. The harvestable risk sits in public-key exchanges – exactly why key establishment carries the 2030 gate.

Migrating a system in 2030 does not recall data an adversary collected in 2026. That changes the deadline.

The Deadline Is Driven by the Data

The concept is captured well by what is often called Mosca’s inequality, from Michele Mosca’s 2015 paper:

Data confidentiality lifetime + migration time > time until a CRQC = the organization is already at risk.

The migration itself takes years and the estimate keeps moving: the Global Risk Institute’s Quantum Threat Timeline Report 2025 puts the probability of a CRQC at 28-49 percent within 10 years and 51-70 percent within 15, up from its prior survey.

We do not need the exact arrival date to manage the risk. We do not wait to learn the date of the next ransomware campaign before building resilience or which credential an adversary will steal before strengthening identity controls. PQC should be treated the same way.

Uncertainty is part of the risk calculation. It is not a reason to postpone it.

Long-Lived Data Changes the Priority

Two systems can use the same vulnerable algorithm and carry completely different quantum risk. Data that loses its sensitivity next year is a different priority than personnel, health, investigative, intellectual-property or national-security information that must stay confidential for 10, 20 or 30 years. M-26-15 already points this way, directing agencies to “prioritize identifying and re-encrypting long-lived sensitive data.” GAO adds a nuance: a CRQC recovers keys slowly – hours to more than 200 hours each – so the adversary’s prize is a long-lived, heavily reused key. Key lifetimes belong in the risk score alongside the algorithm.

A checkbox tells me the control exists. Risk tells me whether it will still work against the threat it is meant to stop.

Discovery Cannot Stay a Spreadsheet Exercise

One department told GAO its unclassified environment supports more than four million endpoints – and it had no plan yet for inventorying the cryptography inside them. M-26-15 calls manual approaches “often insufficient” and directs automated discovery into a central Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM); EO 14412 gives CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) 270 days to publish minimum CBOM elements. Build toward that format now; do not wait for it.

The goal is not simply to complete an inventory. The goal is to create continuous cryptographic visibility.

Testing May Be the Bigger Warning

One GAO finding concerns me even more than inventory: none of the 24 agencies had tested PQC in their environments. ONCD called testing encouraged, not required; GAO’s view is that OMB never called it voluntary and that open-source tooling was enough to begin.

Whatever the policy reading, the engineering reality is the same. PQC migration is not swapping one algorithm for another: larger keys, new handshakes and new libraries ripple through every dependent system, including the legacy ones. Policy now bakes testing into the schedule – M-26-15’s Phase 2 pilots in 2027-2028 and NIST’s own pilot due December 31, 2027 – and NIST has published the standards and the transition path in NIST IR 8547.

"Waiting until the deadline to discover that a critical mission system cannot support the new cryptography is not migration planning. It is crisis management."

— Timothy Amerson, Federal Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), GuidePoint Security

The Point I Keep Coming Back To

Cybersecurity is the Art and Science of Maintaining Operations.

PQC may be the best test of that idea in years. There are two ways to fail. Move too slowly and information protected today may eventually become readable by an adversary. Move without discovery, engineering and testing and we disrupt the mission ourselves. That is why the answer cannot be “move everything immediately.” And it cannot be “we have until 2030.”

Discover. Prioritize. Test. Migrate. Sustain. In that order.

Five Steps to Start PQC Migration Now

If I were sitting with an agency leadership team today, these are the five actions I would put on the board:

Identify the data that must remain sensitive into the 2030s and beyond. That is your highest harvest-now, decrypt-later exposure.

Establish continuous cryptographic discovery. Build toward a living CBOM rather than periodic spreadsheets. Do not wait for a government-furnished tool.

Prioritize by mission risk, data longevity and migration complexity. An HVA designation matters, but it is not the only thing that matters.

Begin representative PQC testing now. Phase 2 pilots start in 2027; the test plan has to exist first.

Connect the migration plan to funding, acquisition and modernization. PQC is not solely a CISO program; M-26-15 names the Chief Financial Officer, program offices and system owners as accountable.

The Federal Government now has policy direction, standards and hard milestones. What agencies cannot afford is to read those milestones as permission to wait.

December 31, 2030 is a compliance deadline. It is not necessarily your risk deadline.

For long-lived sensitive data in transit today, the exposure window may already be open. By 2030, agencies should be measuring what they migrated – not discovering where their vulnerable cryptography lives.

The quantum clock is running. Do not let the calendar make the risk decision for you.

Ready to Start Your PQC Migration?

GuidePoint Security works with Federal agencies and mission partners to assess cryptographic exposure, prioritize systems by mission risk and data longevity and identify discovery, inventory and testing capabilities that fit the environment – without anchoring the strategy to a single vendor. If you cannot yet answer what cryptography you have, what data it protects, how long it must stay protected and what will break when you migrate it, that is where the work begins.

Read Part 1 for the five-phase roadmap, then reach out for a cryptographic exposure assessment.

FAQs

What is harvest now, decrypt later?

Adversaries collect encrypted data today and store it. When a quantum computer arrives, they decrypt it. Data with long confidentiality needs is most at risk.

What is Mosca's inequality?

Mosca’s inequality says data is at risk when its confidentiality lifetime plus migration time exceeds the time until a quantum computer arrives.

How do I start a PQC migration plan?

Begin with a cryptographic inventory using automated discovery tools. Prioritize systems by data longevity and mission risk, then run pilot tests before full migration.

What happens if agencies miss the 2030 PQC deadline?

Data encrypted with vulnerable algorithms stays exposed to harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks. The longer migration takes, the wider the window an adversary has to collect and eventually decrypt sensitive records.

What is a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM)?

A CBOM is a living inventory of all cryptographic assets across an organization. OMB M-26-15 directs agencies to build one using automated discovery rather than manual spreadsheets.

The Third-Party Integrator Risk: OT’s Most Overlooked Attack Surface

November 4, 2026

Austin Turecek

BLOG

5 min.

Industrial Control System (ICS) and operational technology (OT) networks have continued to grow and expand in substantial ways. The demand on the networks have increased as markets have grown, the convergence of IT and OT have changed how these networks look and heightened interest from threat actors have significantly altered the approach to security in these environments.

TL;DR – A third-party integrator can help scale OT environments, but without following best practices, they can also introduce new security risks.

Rapid OT expansion has created the need for third-party support to help manage OT device integration and evolution.

CISA and the FBI highlight the growing exposure risk presented by third-party integrators, which cannot be addressed by least privilege access alone.

By following recommended best practices, including clear documentation, external-facing device reviews, remote access logging, visibility into new and updated devices and manual operations practice, you can reduce the risks associated with third-party integrator support.

Shifts in OT environments have not been small and in many cases, have required third-party support to help manage their evolution effectively. While integrators may help alleviate operational expansion and implement based on new requirements, they also introduce additional risks. Especially if these integrators and their clients don’t enforce proper cyber hygiene.

CISA Highlights the Growing Exposure Risk Created by Third-party Integrators

The OT third-party integrator risk concern was recently called out in a joint publication from CISA and the FBI. This publication “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” highlights the growing exposure of ICS networks and includes a list of recommendations to help assess risk and reduce exposure. While these recommendations follow standard cybersecurity best practices, the historical need for system uptime and reliability has meant these practices sometimes fall on the back burner.

Notably, the core of these security recommendations builds on the “principle of least privilege.” This concept is a core tenet within many organizations, with system administrators restricting users to privileges based on their immediate roles and responsibilities. The goal of these controls is to limit the impact of an attack. If an account or system is breached, the principle of least privilege should minimize the overall reach and impact of an attack.

The Problem with Least Privilege in OT Environments

In reality, the application of “least privilege” poses a significant challenge within OT environments. Many of the foundational protocols, things such as Modbus, DNP3 and older versions of EtherNet/IP lack authentication and role- based access. While this may be difficult within the OT environment due to technical limitations with the basic protocols and the systems in use, additional steps can be taken to limit exposure of critical systems such as the following:

A dedicated integrator access zone or jump host in a DMZ, with no direct path into Purdue Level 1/2 and per-vendor accounts rather than shared integrator credentials

Just-in-time access to reduce the overall exposure of remote access solutions

Enabling MFA on remote access to reduce risks associated with account compromise

Continuous review of accessible user accounts, including integrator and vendor accounts and their activity to ensure permissions are appropriate

Regularly purge stale, unused or deprecated accounts and access as projects close-out

Best Practices When Engaging with Third-party ICS Integrators

In its own publication, CISA also provided a handful of best practices organizations should consider when bringing in third party ICS integrators.

Include Cybersecurity and Supply Chain Cybersecurity in Contracts and Service Agreements

As with all things security, proper implementation needs to start at the beginning. Prior to allowing any third party into your ICS networks, ensure documentation exists, highlight security expectations and accountability. Things such as change management, patching expectations and remote access method documentation can all help organizations understand security practices, even before they begin.

The security of your ICS network doesn’t just rely on your environment, but those that touch it. Proper data hygiene, secure remote access capabilities and documented change management and patch policies all contribute to the security of your environment, even before an integrator steps foot on a factory floor. Additional documentation around steps that will be taken to secure the environment, prior to entering the environment, can help demonstrate and support long term security initiatives.

Evaluate Devices with External Internet Exposure

Internet exposed assets represent a long-lived and frequently exploited path into ICS environments. VPN appliances, cellular modems and internet facing PLCs and HMI all introduce a new avenue of attack.

When working with an integrator, ensure that systems have only the necessary network access. While publicly exposing these systems on the internet may allow for quick and easy management, it also provides threat actors with a low-effort means into the environment. While more effort to configure, secure remote access tools with MFA and no inbound port forwarding can significantly reduce the exposure of a system, while still allowing for robust support.

In addition to configuring secure remote access, regular reviews of your external-facing Ips can help to ensure access in this form isn’t left unchecked.

Monitor and Log Remote Access

Given the criticality of most ICS environments, remote access should be carefully monitored and regularly reviewed. ICS integrators perform important work with ICS environments and as such, these accounts provide a high value entry point into the environment. Unrestricted and unmonitored access can quickly lead to operational blind spots, significantly reducing the environment’s overall integrity.

When possible, organizations should work with integrators to provision “Just-in-Time” access. “Just-in-Time” approval allows for targeted provision access, on approval. As opposed to an always on solution, integrators must request access to a specific system at a specific time. This access can be extended or revoked, at any time.

Access of this nature allows integrators to perform their tasks but also provide the system owners with more granular control. Initial access requires the approval of a trusted legitimate user, reducing the risk of unauthorized access and in the event of a breach or suspicious behavior, the access can quickly be revoked, isolating the overall impact.

In addition to controls such as “Just-in-Time” access, robust logging and monitoring of remote access and sensitive networks can help to identify and flag anomalous behavior. Forwarding logs to an OT aware SIEM can help ensure that alerts are triaged and handled appropriately.

This can easily identify off-hour activity or out-of-scope behavior from integrators. Additionally, consistent passive network monitoring can help identify new integrators systems and devices, even if they aren’t immediately communicated.

Request an Inventory of All Software and Hardware Supplied by the Integrator

Protection begins with visibility. It is impossible to protect the things which you do not know exist. When working with an ICS integrator it is important your team understands the software and hardware they are introducing into the environment.

Each new piece of software and hardware introduces a new potential means of compromise. An asset inventory supports vulnerability management and helps teams choose between patching and compensating controls. Undocumented software or hardware can quickly fall out of date and introduce new vulnerabilities in the environment.

Additionally, logic output should also be requested. PLC project and logic files, system backs ups and any integrator tool should also be collected and understood. These files and components create an actionable audit trail that can be leveraged to ensure system and environment integrity.

Practice Procedures and Maintain Capabilities for Manual Operations

ICS integrators can become a core part of an organization’s operations. In these situations, it’s important to ensure that they understand their roles and responsibilities within the organization.

Regular reviews with integrators can ensure they are ready and able to perform any necessary manual operations and fail-safe procedures. When performing tabletop exercises, reviewing policy and maintaining daily operations, these integrators should be present to ensure they are available and ready in the event of an incident.

The following list several best practices that should be regularly reviewed and verified with integrators.

Appropriate change management controls when interacting with and modifying PLCs logic. System owners should work with integrators and manage policy, to ensure that a reliable fallback logic is available and new logic is properly documented.

Policy exists to ensure that integrator-owned systems are regularly scanned to mitigate risks of malware.

Effective off boarding procedures should be in place to ensure inactive integrator accounts and systems cannot be used for an attack. Disable accounts and ensure unused systems/software are removed.

Ensure appropriate controls and segmentation exist between remote access solutions and high priority safety systems.

Start with a Risk Assessment

Outside of following these recommendations, regular risk assessments are highly encouraged. While some integrators have always put security first and built the systems and environments they support with this in mind, others may have focused their efforts on operational reliance and performance. The use of default credentials, insecure network configurations, outdated and vulnerable software and insufficient documentation is common in some ICS environments.

In these situations it is important to have a trusted partner capable of not only validating past work but also helping to support and foster an environment of operational and security excellence. GuidePoint’s consultants and engineers are well positioned to help organizations establish an OT security baseline so they can grow securely.

FAQs

What happens when a third-party integrator is compromised in an OT environment?

A compromised integrator account can give attackers direct access to controllers and sensors that run physical processes. Lateral movement from an integrator’s entry point can bypass IT security controls entirely. The impact ranges from production downtime to safety incidents depending on the attacker’s objectives.

How should organizations vet third-party ICS integrators before granting access?

Start with documented security requirements in the contract before any access is provisioned. Request evidence of the integrator’s own security practices including patch management and remote access policies. Verify that the integrator can support your logging and monitoring requirements.

What is the CISA advisory on third-party ICS integrators?

CISA and the FBI published “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators” in 2026. The advisory highlights the growing exposure of ICS networks through third-party access. It recommends applying least privilege controls and monitoring all integrator activity.

Why is unmonitored remote access dangerous in ICS environments?

Unmonitored remote sessions create blind spots where unauthorized changes can go undetected. Persistent VPN tunnels and always-on connections give attackers a low-effort entry point into critical systems. Without session logging, organizations cannot trace the source or scope of a breach.

October 30, 2026 – Published on The Wall Street Journal

Corporate cybersecurity leaders are having a schadenfreude moment after Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, lost billions of dollars this week to hackers.

Cryptocurrencies, like bitcoin, Ethereum and hundreds of others, have become the financial engine for ransomware attacks. By offering cybercriminals both speed and anonymity for collecting ransom payments, digital currencies have helped make ransomware into a booming underworld industry—and a major headache for chief information security officers.

On Thursday, Binance suspended transactions after hackers broke into the exchange’s platform and took off with more than $6 billion, marking the biggest cyber heist in history. The company said it is currently investigating the attack, which appears to have accessed systems through a worker’s laptop.

Ransomware attacks are now a leading cybersecurity threat, with many pointing to the rise of crypto as an enabler. But crypto isn’t the only factor behind the rise of the ransomware market. Among other issues, increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, new and wide-scale security vulnerabilities exposed by artificial intelligence and mounting geopolitical tensions have all played a role, cybersecurity experts say.Jason Baker, threat intelligence practice lead at GuidePoint Security, a cybersecurity services and incident response firm that helps companies negotiate with ransomware hackers, said crypto is a convenient scapegoat for beleaguered security chiefs.“You don’t blame cars if they’re the getaway vehicle for a bank robbery,” Baker said. And just as banning cars wouldn’t prevent bank robberies, he said, shutting down crypto platforms won’t stop hackers. “Threat actors adapt, and while this is a tool they’re used to, I think they’d adapt further away from cryptocurrency if they had to,” Baker said.Read More HERE.

What Happens Next: Turn Cloud Security Assessment Findings Into Action

October 28, 2026

Adrian Pascual

BLOG

5 min.

Cloud security assessments are good at finding problems. Once the assessment is over? That’s where things can get complicated.

An assessment may identify excessive permissions, exposed data, insecure configurations, gaps around AI or weaknesses in how an application is protected. The report gets delivered, everyone agrees the findings are important and then a much harder question comes up: Who actually owns fixing this?

That answer matters, because a cloud security finding is rarely just a “cloud problem.”

TL;DR – The real value of a cloud security assessment is what follows the report: contextual prioritization, assigning ownership and resolution of the findings.

Cloud findings can be as complex as cloud environments themselves, with multiple stakeholders and responsible parties.

Contextual analysis and prioritization require cross-functional conversations and collaboration.

Turning findings into action that often requires expertise beyond the team that performed the original assessment.

Start With The Environment

It might seem natural to assume that a “cloud finding” means “cloud security” owns remediation. Reality often dictates a much different view.

Some issues may be superficial, such as an unrestricted security group on an isolated dev instance. The cloud security team can probably fix this one without broader coordination. Other issues may involve multiple stakeholders and require engineering support from a team of domain experts before they can be truly considered fixed.

One of the universal realities of cloud security is how interconnected everything has become.

Take an identity finding in a cloud environment: An overprivileged service account maintains persistent credentials and lacks a defined rotation policy. At first glance, it might seem straightforward. Bring in the identity team, scope the permissions and enforce least-privilege policies.

But what if that service account has access to unencrypted personally identifiable information (PII) or financial records that are subject to Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) regulations? Now data security matters. And so does compliance.

What if the same identity is also connected to a customer-facing application programming interface (API) gateway that serves production traffic? Now the application security team needs to get involved. Possibly the developers as well.

Now let’s complicate it even further. What if an AI service is using that service account to pull training data or take action based on customer inputs? Now AI security enters the conversation and compliance adds additional checks.

The blast radius has now extended beyond the cloud platform, into identity and access management (IAM), through data security, across compliance in multiple ways and into model integrity, prompt injection risks and data lineage obligations.

And if there is evidence that the exposure may already have been abused, the conversation may quickly move toward the security operations center (SOC) or incident response team.

The cloud team who initially received the finding of “an overprivileged identity” is now responsible for remediation across multiple teams.

The original finding has not changed. The context around it has. That is why one team cannot realistically be expected to solve every security issue uncovered during an assessment. Understanding the complete environment touched by a finding will help determine who actually owns remediation.

What’s the Best Process to Determine Ownership of Cloud Security Remediation?

The best way to determine who owns what is to know who’s who among your experts and lean into that expertise. I tend to think about this process the same way I think about tools. You would not use a screwdriver to hammer a nail into a wall. You use the right tool for the job. Security expertise works the same way. The value of a finding depends entirely on whether the right person is interpreting it.

If the assessment uncovers significant identity weaknesses, involve someone who understands identity architecture and access controls.

If the findings involve sensitive information, data governance, classification or exposure, bring in data security expertise.

If application architecture is contributing to the risk, involve the application security team.

If the concern is operational detection or evidence of compromise, involve the SOC or incident response team.

If AI is part of the environment, there may be entirely new questions around identities, permissions, applications, data access and governance.

Not every finding will involve five different teams. However, organizations that avoid assuming the team that finds the problem is automatically the team best equipped to solve it tend to resolve findings faster and more effectively. Ownership clarity accelerates remediation. Ambiguity stalls it.

What if My Team Lacks the Experts Needed to Analyze Findings?

This is more common than most organizations admit and it is not a failure. It’s simply a resourcing reality.

Many security teams operate lean. They have strong generalists who keep operations running, but they do not have deep specialists in every domain an assessment might touch. Identity architecture, data governance, application security and AI security are just a few of the distinct disciplines within the larger cybersecurity knowledge sphere and very few organizations staff all of them internally.

The risk is in treating findings as resolved when the team analyzing them does not fully understand the implications. A generalist reviewing an identity finding might close it as low-priority because the immediate access looks limited, while a specialist would recognize that the same misconfiguration creates a lateral movement opportunity across the environment.

There are a few ways organizations navigate this gap:

Engage External Specialists for Targeted Analysis: A third-party assessment partner can provide the domain expertise a finding requires without the overhead of a full-time hire. This is particularly effective for complex identity, data security or AI-related findings where internal knowledge may be thin.

Build Relationships Before You Need Them: Organizations that establish partnerships with specialized security firms ahead of an assessment can move faster when findings land. The alternative (scrambling to find expertise after a critical finding surfaces) introduces delays at potentially inopportune times.

Use Findings to Identify Capability Gaps: If every assessment produces findings that sit unresolved because no one internally can fully interpret them, that pattern is itself a finding. It reveals where the organization needs to invest, whether through hiring, upskilling or advisory relationships.

Separate Interpretation From Remediation: Even when internal teams will execute the fix, the initial analysis and prioritization can come from external expertise. This keeps remediation timelines tight while ensuring findings are understood in full context before action begins.

The goal is to have a path to the right answer for every finding, whether that path runs through internal teams, external partners or a combination of both.

How Do I Determine Which Findings to Fix First?

Now you have identified the environment and stakeholders for your findings. So you should simply tackle them based on severity score, right?

Not quite.

At this stage, contextual analysis continues to matter. This is also where many remediation processes lose steam.

A finding tells us something exists. A severity rating tells us how someone scored it. Neither of those tells us what to do about it or more importantly: what happens if we do nothing.

Once we understand the environment around a finding (the systems it touches, the data it exposes, the access it enables, etc.) and we know who needs to be involved in the remediation process, then we need to answer some pointed contextual questions:

Does it need to be fixed immediately?

Do we have all of the information or are there outstanding unknowns that require additional investigation?

Do we have a process for coordinating between all involved teams?

Are there mitigating controls already in place?

Is the risk understood and accepted?

Is the finding pointing to a deeper, systemic weakness or architectural design flaw?

What is the risk if we do nothing or postpone the fix?

Answers to questions such as these provide a much more useful prioritization outcome than simply labeling something High, Medium or Low and moving on.

The Assessment Is a Starting Point

An assessment report can document hundreds of findings. Your auditors need your reports. That alone does not necessarily make the organization safer, yet there is a tendency to view the final report as the end of an assessment.

There is a different way to see it: Real strides in security posture maturity are made when the report becomes the basis for a clearer understanding of the environment and creating a practical path forward:

Finding → Context → Priority → Owner → Action

The strongest security programs succeed by deciding what each finding means, bringing the right people into the conversation and then doing something about it.

Finding the issue is important, but knowing what to do next is where the real value begins.

FAQs

What is blast radius in cloud security?

Blast radius describes how far a single security finding can extend across an environment. An overprivileged service account, for example, can span identity, data security, compliance and application security — turning one finding into a cross-functional remediation effort.

What is the difference between a severity score and contextual risk?

A severity score rates a finding in isolation. Contextual risk accounts for what systems the finding touches, what data it exposes and what happens if you do nothing. Effective prioritization requires both.

Should you use the same team for assessment and remediation?

Not necessarily. The team that identifies a finding may not have the domain expertise to resolve it. Separating interpretation from remediation ensures findings are fully understood before action begins.

Any change large enough to invalidate the assumptions of your last assessment. Common triggers include mergers and acquisitions, major workload migrations, new AI platform deployments and security incidents that reveal gaps in detection or access controls.

What happens if cloud security findings go unresolved?

Unresolved findings compound over time. Configuration drift widens the gap and institutional knowledge degrades. What started as a single misconfiguration can become a systemic exposure across identity, data and application layers.

The Identities Nobody Is Governing Are About to Rotate Every 47 Days

October 27, 2026

Mark Whitesell

BLOG

5 min.

TL;DR – Public Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate validity drops to 100 days in March 2027 and 47 days by 2029. Certificates are non-human credentials and organizations that lack full discovery and automated lifecycle management will face recurring outages, compliance gaps and tougher cyber insurance renewals.

Three takeaways:

Certificates are identity, not infrastructure. If your certificate program is not part of your identity governance framework, you have a blind spot that shrinks with every validity reduction.

Most organizations only track what their primary CA issues are. Certificates from cloud providers, containers and shadow IT teams sit outside that view.

March 2027 is an automation deadline, not a compliance checkbox. At 100-day validity, manual renewal processes break at enterprise scale. Organizations that invest in discovery and automation now will absorb the transition. Those that wait will spend Q1 in reactive mode.

It’s Wednesday morning and your VP of Engineering pings the security channel: a production API gateway is rejecting connections. So the team runs through the usual checks: Traffic is flowing. DNS is clean. Firewall rules haven’t changed.

Forty minutes later, someone finds the source. A Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate on an internal service expired overnight. It was issued eleven months ago by a team that has since reorged and it was never added to your renewal tracker.

This outage is not unusual and the root cause is always the same, a credential no one was watching. That scenario plays out today with certificates valid for a year or more. Now compress the timeline.

The Timeline is Already Moving

March 15, 2026: the CA/Browser Forum’s Ballot SC-081v3 took effect, capping public TLS certificate validity at 200 days. This is the current state.

March 15, 2027: the next milestone drops the maximum to 100 days. Manual certificate management breaks at this cadence.

March 15, 2029: every publicly trusted certificate tops out at 47 days. There is no opt-out. Every publicly trusted certificate authority is bound by this schedule.

SC-081v3 applies specifically to publicly trusted TLS certificates, but the operational implications extend across your entire Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) environment. Organizations managing TLS renewals manually are almost certainly managing internal certificates, code signing and machine identities the same way. The validity reduction is a TLS mandate. The readiness gap it exposes is a PKI-wide problem.

For organizations still managing certificates manually, the math is unforgiving. At 47-day validity, a single certificate requires nearly eight renewals per year. Multiply that across hundreds or thousands of certificates, many of which have never been inventoried and the operational burden becomes unsustainable without automation. Organizations need to adapt now or timelines will catch up.

This is Not a Web Certificate Problem

It is tempting to treat shortened certificate lifecycles as a web server issue, something your infrastructure team handles during routine maintenance windows. But that framing misses the scope of what is actually at stake.

Certificates authenticate actions on behalf of humans and non-human identities, including service accounts, API connections, cloud workloads, CI/CD pipelines and AI agents. Every time one of these identities establishes trust with another system, a certificate is doing the work.

When a certificate expires untracked, it does not generate a security alert. It generates:

An outage

Authentication chains break

Automated workflows stop

Production systems go offline

And the team that gets the 2:00 AM call spends hours tracing the failure to a credential that was issued once, never inventoried and never assigned to an owner.

At 200 days, that risk is manageable in small environments. At 47 days, it becomes a recurring operational failure for any organization without automation.

The Discovery Gap

Organizations assume they know how many certificates they have because they track what their primary certificate authority issues. That view misses certificates issued by cloud providers, embedded in containers, baked into legacy applications or managed by individual engineering teams outside of central IT.

The gap between “what we think we have” and “what actually exists” is where both outages and risk concentrate. You cannot rotate what you can’t see and you cannot assign ownership to something you don’t know about.

IDC research sponsored by GuidePoint Security found that abused non-human identities are now tied as the top entry point in confirmed breaches and only a fraction of organizations run continuous discovery across their non-human identity landscape. Certificates are non-human credentials. If organizations are not discovering service accounts and API keys, they are almost certainly not discovering every certificate in their environment either.

That’s the disconnect shortened lifecycles will force into the open. Organizations that treat certification management as a separate infrastructure function (detached from their identity governance program) are building a slot spot at the exact same moment that the rotation window is shrinking.

What Shortened Certificate Lifecycles Mean for Cyber Insurance

Cyber insurance carriers are tightening underwriting requirements around security hygiene and cryptographic infrastructure is part of that evolution. Expired or mismanaged certificates create two categories of risk that underwriters care about:

Attack surface exposure (man-in-the-middle, impersonation)

Operational liability (outages, compliance failures, downtime)

If you are approaching a cyber insurance renewal, expect more pointed questions about how you manage certificate lifecycles, whether rotation is automated and whether you can demonstrate control maturity across your cryptographic environment. The ability to answer those questions directly affects coverage of those terms.

What to Do Before March 2027

The 100-day milestone is less than six months away. Here’s what you need to do before March 2027:

Run a certificate discovery assessment

Map every certificate to an owner

Evaluate automation readiness

Connect certificates to your identity program

Pressure-test your incident response

Assess your post-quantum cryptography readiness

What to Do Before March 2027

If you’re not starting to plan for March 2027 now, you will spend Q1 scrambling to get a hold of your environments. Those that take the time now to discover what they have, automate what they can and assign ownership for the rest, will operate with few outages, less risk and a stronger security posture.

Your certificate infrastructure is your trust infrastructure. The countdown is already running.

Ready to assess your certificate landscape? Schedule time with our identity team to get started.

FAQs

Why are TLS certificate lifecycles getting shorter?

The CA/Browser Forum passed Ballot SC-081v3, which reduces public TLS certificate validity to 200 days (2026), 100 days (2027) and 47 days (2029). Every publicly trusted certificate authority is bound by this schedule. Shorter validity windows reduce the time an attacker can use a compromised certificate.

Why are certificates considered non-human identities?

Certificates authenticate machines, services and workloads the same way passwords authenticate people. They are credentials assigned to non-human entities like APIs, containers and CI/CD pipelines. Managing them outside your identity program creates a blind spot that becomes more dangerous with every validity reduction.

How does certificate automation reduce outage risk?

Automated certificate lifecycle management handles discovery and renewal without manual intervention. At 47-day validity, a single certificate needs nearly eight renewals per year. Without automation, each renewal is a manual task where human error can cause an outage.

What happens if you don't automate certificate renewals before March 2027?

At 100-day validity, manual renewal processes break at enterprise scale. Expired certificates cause outages, break authentication chains and stall automated workflows. Organizations without automation will spend Q1 2027 in reactive mode instead of operating normally.

How do expired certificates affect cyber insurance renewals?

Carriers are tightening underwriting requirements around security hygiene. Expired or mismanaged certificates create two categories of risk: attack surface exposure and operational liability. The ability to demonstrate automated certificate lifecycle management directly affects coverage terms.
