AI Agents Don’t Stop at the Device. Your Security Program Shouldn’t Either.

October 26, 2026

GuidePoint Security

By Chris Hughes, VP Security Strategy, Noma

BLOG

5 min.

AI agents don’t need an exploit to cause damage. They just need permission, something most security teams already granted, one login at a time.

Why Is This Suddenly a Governance Problem?

AI agents have moved from experimental to running daily workflows on employee devices. Developers use coding agents to inspect repositories, run terminal commands and open pull requests. Business users deploy productivity agents to search documents, draft emails and update CRM records, extending both with MCP servers, skills and connectors often installed from public registries in minutes, with no review process.

No single action here is dangerous on its own. The agent inherits permissions to everything the employee running it can reach: credentials, browser sessions, internal systems, even production infrastructure and a config edit or a linked account can extend that reach before security has any record of the change.

The device isn’t the end of the story. A coding agent that starts on a laptop can call a homegrown service or cloud API. A productivity agent can move from local files into a SaaS platform in the same task. The device is where the agent launches, not the boundary of what it can reach.

TL;DR – AI agents can use an employee’s access to carry out tasks across enterprise systems. Individually authorized actions can combine into data exposure risk or destructive changes that single-event controls miss and the full sequence often runs beyond the device where the agent started.

Key Takeaways:

Agents already operate with the same access as the people running them, extended further by MCP servers, skills and connectors.

Risk usually comes from a sequence of individually legitimate actions, often crossing from the device into SaaS and homegrown systems.

Closing the gap means extending the visibility security teams already have on the endpoint into one model that follows an agent everywhere it goes.

When Does Legitimate Agent Activity Become Risky?

An agent can use an approved application, act on behalf of an authenticated user and make permitted API calls while still exposing sensitive data or making destructive changes. The risk becomes clear only when you look at how those actions connect across the full session.

Consider a desktop agent handling routine CRM follow-ups: one lead record contains instructions to email account history and contact details to an external address. The agent follows those instructions, though they came from the record rather than the user. The query, the data access and the email tool were each authorized on their own. Only connecting the untrusted instruction to the data pull and the outbound send reveals how a routine task became data exposure, starting on a device and ending through a SaaS application.

Agent risk is often distributed across a sequence of actions that each look fine in isolation and increasingly, across more than one environment.

What Are the Recurring Failure Modes?

A few patterns show up again and again as organizations adopt agents:

Shadow agents and configuration drift

Employees install a new assistant or MCP server to finish a task, then move on, leaving the configuration behind long after anyone is tracking it.

Personal account connections

Agents can authenticate through personal accounts on the same device used for work, creating a path for company data to cross identity boundaries outside enterprise administration.

Excessive permissions

A connector added for one read-only task can just as easily expose write, delete or administrative functions the job never required, a pattern OWASP names directly as Excessive Agency in its Top 10 for LLM Applications.

Supply chain exposure

Every MCP server, skill and connector an agent uses can be misconfigured, compromised or quietly updated after it was first reviewed.

In one documented case, a widely used coding CLI was found uploading entire local repositories, commit history included, to the vendor’s own cloud storage, independent of what the model had actually read.

Prompt injection and tool poisoning

Agents process natural language from sources they don’t control: web pages, tickets, code comments, tool responses. For example, instructions hidden in an MCP tool’s own description can silently redirect an agent’s actions.

None of these require a sophisticated attacker. They’re the result of giving autonomous software the same reach and access as a trusted employee, without the judgment a human applies.

Extending Endpoint Visibility Across the Full Agent Estate

Endpoint-focused discovery and control are the right starting point: they tell security teams which agents, MCP servers and skills are actually running on employee devices.

The opportunity is to carry that same visibility to where an agent’s activity actually goes. In the CRM example above, the agent launched from a desktop, but the exposure happened when data moved to an external recipient through a SaaS-based email tool. Connecting an agent’s local footprint to its identity, destination and behavior across SaaS and homegrown systems is what turns endpoint visibility into full protection.

Security teams get the most value by extending what they already have on the endpoint with a unified policy model and behavioral baseline that follows an agent into every environment it reaches, so the same identity, rules and audit trail apply wherever the agent runs.

How Should Security Teams Respond?

Locking agents down entirely isn’t realistic. The goal is bringing every agent, wherever it runs, into one governance model that builds on endpoint visibility.

1. Build a live inventory across every environment

You can’t govern agents, MCP servers and skills you don’t know exist. Discovery should cover what’s actively running and what’s configured but dormant, since a dormant component can become active the moment an agent invokes it.

2. Apply least-privilege access control consistently

Govern which MCP servers, tools and skills agents can use based on identity and group membership and scope permissions to individual tools and actions so access to a system doesn’t automatically include write, delete or admin rights.

3. Set business-defined boundaries that follow the agent, not the environment

Some risk depends on cumulative effect, not any single action, like a refund agent with no daily cap. Those limits need to hold regardless of where the agent is invoked from.

4. Detect and stop risky behavior across the full session

An agent may encounter a prompt injection, retrieve sensitive data and attempt to send it outside the company minutes later through a connected SaaS application. Security needs to connect those actions and intervene while the task is underway.

5. Establish ownership and identity context from day one

Know who owns each agent, whose credentials it uses and which tools and skills are approved for that user or group, with ownership, review status and approvals managed under one model.

6. Build toward a single control plane

As agents show up in new places, from endpoint devices to SaaS platforms to homegrown systems, the organizations getting this right consolidate around one policy model and one behavioral baseline that extends their existing endpoint investment to follow an agent wherever it runs.

So Where Do You Go From Here?

Effective agent governance brings discovery, identity-based access control, business-defined boundaries and runtime enforcement into one model across endpoint, SaaS and homegrown agents, extending the visibility security teams have already built rather than replacing it.

This is the kind of work GuidePoint Security helps organizations operationalize: connecting existing identity, endpoint and access governance programs to cover agents and the systems they reach, with consistent policies and a clear process for responding when activity becomes risky.

The organizations managing this well are the ones who treated agent governance as one identity and access problem from the start, covering endpoint, SaaS and homegrown agents under a single model rather than solving each surface on its own.

Agents aren’t going away and neither is the access they’ve already inherited. The question isn’t whether to let employees use them. It’s whether security has one consistent answer, across every environment, to what those agents can reach, what they’re allowed to do and how you’d know if that changed.

By The GuidePoint Security Cloud Team

BLOG

TL;DR

AWS Security Hub Extended lets customers bring AWS native detection and partner tools together, with findings normalized for correlation

Results depend on what sits underneath: architecture and risk priorities, a secure AWS foundation and a plan for AI

GuidePoint joined as a services partner to help customers settle those fundamentals first

Security teams often manage products that were selected at different times for different problems. Each can generate useful data, but connecting findings across endpoint, identity, data, cloud and other domains often falls to the people operating them.

Amazon Web Services Security Hub Extended addresses part of that challenge by giving customers a single AWS experience to review and subscribe to curated partner solutions. Participating solutions emit findings using the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and AWS Security Hub aggregates those findings so teams can examine risks that span domains.

GuidePoint Security recently joined AWS Security Hub Extended as a services partner. Our role is to work with customers on how those capabilities fit their environments, prepare the AWS foundations that support them and integrate selected technologies into day-to-day security operations. We start with each customer’s architecture, existing investments, risk priorities and operating model.

Security Hub Extended can simplify several parts of adopting security technology. AWS serves as the seller of record for participating partner solutions and customers can review offerings and initiate subscriptions from the Security Hub console.

It creates a shared way to bring findings together. Standardizing data in OCSF reduces the translation work required to examine activity across tools and gives security teams more context when a risk crosses traditional product boundaries.

A broader set of integrated tools also introduces choices about coverage, overlap, deployment and ownership. Customers need to confirm that each addition addresses an actual gap, fits the current technology stack and sends new findings into established response processes.

Start With Architecture and Risk

Security technology decisions are most useful when they are tied to defined risks and use cases. Before selecting additional tools, organizations should establish a current view of their AWS environment and the controls already in place.

Start by mapping:

Sources of security findings

AWS and third-party technologies already deployed

Overlaps and gaps in coverage

Ownership of investigation and response

Planned cloud migrations and AI adoption belong in the same view because they can change identity, data and governance requirements. AI is one of 10 security domains in Security Hub Extended, which makes it a practical place to start a readiness conversation. An AI readiness assessment evaluates AI security and governance considerations and sets priorities before adoption expands.

The result should be a prioritized set of security requirements that gives security, cloud and procurement teams a common foundation for evaluating the options available through AWS Security Hub Extended.

Build on a Secure AWS Foundation

Identity, logging, account governance, network controls and configuration standards shape how reliably tools can be deployed across AWS and how much context is available when a finding needs investigation. Confirm account governance, access management and telemetry collection, then check that guardrails apply across workloads. This matters most during migration, when inherited configurations and compressed timelines can create uneven controls.

GuidePoint helps customers build this layer with services such as AWS Control Tower, Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Security Lake. Addressing it early gives partner technologies a stable environment and can reduce rework during deployment.

Keep Calm and Patch PHP2Shell

October 21, 2026

Justin Timothy

With contributions by the GuidePoint Security GRIT team

BLOG

10 min.

How to Respond to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

*Note: This is an actively developing situation and the information from this blog is accurate as of writing. Please refer to PHP’s official guidance for any newly released information and additional patching and mitigation recommendations.

The newly released ‘PHP2Shell’ vulnerabilities have become a hot topic hitting the desks, feeds and wires of every cybersecurity professional around the world. Starting October 20th, leaked details, disputed PoCs, conflicting exploitation reports and a patch that was scheduled but not yet released started circulating among security professionals online.

TL;DR – LPHP2Shell is a critical, highly exploitable set of two vulnerabilities that could potentially affect a massive percentage of internet facing websites. The patch is available and the time to patch is now.

CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively nicknamed “PHP2Shell”, are critical severity vulnerabilities that require immediate attention.

Patches are available for supported versions of PHP. PHP supplied Linux distributions and LTS vendors the patches in advance. Experts recommend isolating or decommissioning systems running versions older than 7.4.

It’s important to patch internet-facing systems first, rebuild containers that contain PHP, restart all affected systems after patching and conduct retrospective threat hunts to ensure no threat actors slipped through before the patches were applied.

The instinct during these types of high-impact vulnerability disclosures is to either panic or wait for certainty. Panic can lead to uncoordinated patching and inconsistent workarounds. Waiting means the exploit code is circulating before you hit your change window.

It wasn’t until PHP released their official post announcing the two CVEs and the mitigation options that the world was able to definitively understand the impact and start implementing patch management strategies.

This is why a balanced approach works best: act on what’s confirmed, prepare for what’s coming and make deliberate decisions about the tradeoffs you’re accepting.

What We Know About PHP2Shell

All PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed are affected by these vulnerabilities. PHP considers the risk highest for mod_php, where the demonstrated exploit achieves unauthenticated remote code execution before application code runs. Both CVEs have been rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0 by PHP.

CVE-2026-109618: RCE via OOM Corruption

PHP handles out-of-memory (OOM) conditions, unwinding straight out of the current execution context and aborting the request. In certain early-request contexts, request-scoped memory is reachable before it has been fully initialized.

If any allocation fails in that window, the non-local exit skips the initialization and PHP’s error path does not account for the half-built state. The request shutdown routine then reads or branches on that memory. The failing allocation does not need to be related to the corrupted memory, so the trigger is generic: any OOM during the window is enough.

Several OOM-induction strategies trigger it consistently, which makes exploitation reliable and leads to Remote Code Execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109619: RCE Via Stale Global State

PHP workers are long-lived and reused across requests and they keep some global state (error, session, object and extension data) that points to memory belonging to a single request. That state should be cleared before the request’s memory is freed. A fatal error can stop an operation before it cleans up.

Examples include running out of memory, hitting the execution time limit or a failed compile. A later warning during shutdown can also refill error state that was already cleared. The request’s memory is then freed while the worker still points to it, which is a use-after-free. When the same worker handles its next request, early steps that run before normal setup (input, configuration, session and error handling) can read, free or act on that stale pointer.

With a carefully crafted memory layout, an attacker can turn this into RCE, meaning they run their own code on the server. Exploitation takes two separate HTTP requests handled by the same worker: the first leaves stale state behind and the second uses it.

PHP2Shell encompasses two critical-severity vulnerabilities in one of the most widely deployed server-side runtimes on the internet. A patch has now been made available and we encourage all organizations to patch where possible.

Why PHP2Shell Deserves Your Attention

Not every vulnerability warrants immediate attention; however, this one does. The characteristics, including the potential impact and the exploitability demand quick action.

The parsing layer is the attack surface: Initial reporting indicates that the PHP2Shell vulnerability triggers during multipart/form-data parsing, before your application code executes. CMS maintenance modes, security plugins, authentication layers… none of it matters once it’s under attack. The request body gets parsed by PHP itself and that’s where the flaw lives.

The affected footprint is potentially enormous: PHP powers a significant portion of global websites with their server-side language. It’s embedded in WordPress, cPanel, WHM, Laravel-based internal tools, hosting panels, appliances and countless containerized microservices. Many organizations running PHP don’t think of themselves as PHP shops.

End-of-life PHP versions won’t get a fix: PHP 8.1 and earlier are considered end-of-life by the vendor. Any system running a legacy PHP version will not receive an official patch. If the claims about the vulnerability affecting versions as far back as PHP 5, many systems may face the need for rapid upgrade or decommissioning to ensure security.

The exploit interest is high and the details are public: The advisories are linked, the root causes are documented and the confirmed attack paths are described. The window between “patch available” and “weaponized exploit code circulating” is narrowing. We know from experience that threat actors weaponize large scale, public exploits within 24-48 hours of their disclosure.

How to Patch PHP2Shell

PHP has released the following versions that have addressed the vulnerabilities: PHP 8.5.12, PHP 8.4.27, PHP 8.3.36 and PHP 8.2.35.

Source downloads are available on php.net. Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so check your vendor for updated packages.

Patching alone does not fully mitigate the possibility of exploitation. Keep in mind exploitability and follow this recommended execution sequence to reduce the highest risks first:

Patch internet-facing systems first: With systems that face the internet, the attack surface is remote and unauthenticated. Internet-facing PHP hosts are the front line. Secure them before all others to close the widest gap.

Confirm the fix through package changelogs, not version strings: Distributions frequently backport security fixes without changing the upstream version number. A system reporting PHP 8.4.26 might already contain the fix if the distribution backported it. Check the package changelog or the distribution’s security advisory for confirmation.

Restart everything: Patching the binary on disk doesn’t protect running processes. Restart PHP-FPM, Apache modules and every long-running PHP process. This includes queue workers, schedulers and daemons. Without a restart, these processes continue running the old, vulnerable binary.

Rebuild and redeploy container images: If PHP runs in containers, updating the host package isn’t enough. Rebuild images with the patched PHP version and redeploy. Every running container based on the old image remains vulnerable.

Watch your distribution’s timeline: Not every package repository will have the fix today. The volunteer-run Remi repository (widely used on RHEL-based servers) will not publish updates on October 21st. PHP’s advisory urges Remi users to switch to distribution packages or build from source so the fix can be applied immediately.

What to Do If You Can't Patch PHP2Shell Immediately

PHP’s guidance is clear: the only complete solution is an update.

PHP has published specific interim measures that reduce exposure to confirmed attack paths. These mitigations are not equivalent to patching. They mitigate the risk of exploitation, but they do not eliminate it completely.

The multi-part rejection workaround remains valid as an additional layer for both CVEs. Rejecting requests whose Content-Type contains multipart/form-data at the web server, before they reach PHP, is still a strong stopgap. Cover all HTTP methods, not just POST (PHP 8.4+ parses multipart bodies on other methods) and apply it to every virtual host and default server that passes requests to PHP. This breaks file uploads until removed.

For CVE-2026-109618 (OOM corruption):

Set memory_limit=-1, preferably in a way applications can’t override (e.g., php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration). Verify that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

Set a low post_max_size. For applications that don’t require file uploads, post_max_size = 8M. If file uploads are necessary, post_max_size = 32M. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size. Enforce limits at the web server or proxy level for decoded request size, input field count, multipart part count, header count and nesting depth, including for requests without a usable Content-Length.

Use a container or cgroup limit as an availability boundary, preferably with a policy that kills only the affected worker. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, as these can cause vulnerable allocation failure.

For CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state):

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and restart every worker. Use php.ini, an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Do not rely on ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. The setting needs to take effect before the parser runs.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal backtrace path only.

Remove invalid or deprecated settings applied per request that emit diagnostics before initialization. Hiding diagnostics with error_reporting, display_errors or @ does not help.

The Systems That Won't Get an Official Fix (But Might Get Help)

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life, so normally, those versions would not receive updates. Notably, PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 to help organizations building from source or without access to an LTS vendor. This is not a full-support commitment. However, it is a valuable lifeline for teams that can compile from source and need to close the gap.

For systems that can’t be patched or compiled from backports (and especially for anything older than 7.4) the guidance from multiple regulatory boards and industry experts stands: isolate internet-facing PHP systems from public networks or take them offline entirely. That’s a hard conversation for teams running legacy applications on unsupported PHP versions and it’s a conversation that needs to happen today.

With a widely available patch for supported versions and the lifeline thrown for some legacy code, threat actors will weaponize these exploits against unpatched and end of life systems.

After Patching: Hunt Backwards

Patching closes the door, which reduces your risk going forward. However, it doesn’t guarantee that a threat actor wasn’t able to slip through the cracks while you were busy patching. A retrospective threat hunt based on these behavior signals can help you eliminate the possibility of infiltration:

PHP worker child processes spawning shells or download utilities (PHP-FPM, Apache or other PHP workers)

Unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs (plausible side effects of memory-corruption exploitation attempts)

Unusual multipart/form-data requests from October 20th, 15:00 UTC onward, particularly to endpoints that don’t accept uploads

New or modified files in web roots, upload directories, plugin directories and mu-plugins

Changes to .user.ini files or the auto_prepend_file setting

Persistence indicators: new cron entries, systemd units, Supervisor entries, SSH authorized_keys additions, newly created application admin accounts or unexpected outbound connections from PHP service accounts

A clean result doesn’t rule out compromise, but it does indicate that the available behavioral indicators didn’t fire. That’s a meaningful data point. That said: preserve your logs. Web server and PHP logs from October 20th, 15:00 UTC onward are your forensic baseline. Log rotation, redeployment and container rebuilds can destroy the evidence needed for a compromise assessment. Back them up before patching changes anything.

Stay Tuned for Updates

GuidePoint Security’s GRIT team is actively tracking PHP2Shell and its impact. We will provide updated advisories, emerging exploit techniques and confirmed indicators of compromise as they become available. If PHP workers are spawning shells, unexpected files appear in web roots or you discover persistence mechanisms on a PHP host, the GuidePoint Security Incident Response team is ready to help.

FAQs

What is PHP2Shell?

PHP2Shell is the collective name for two critical PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) disclosed on October 20, 2026. Both are rated CVSS 9.2 (Critical) and can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on PHP web servers. CVE-2026-109618 exploits out-of-memory corruption during request processing and CVE-2026-109619 exploits stale global state that persists across requests within the same PHP worker process.

What PHP versions are affected by PHP2Shell?

All PHP installations serving web requests are affected, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP considers mod_php the highest-risk configuration. Patched versions are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life and will not receive official patches, though PHP published minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1. Unconfirmed reports indicate the vulnerabilities may affect versions as far back as PHP 5.

How do I patch PHP2Shell?

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Source downloads are available on php.net and Linux distributions and LTS vendors received patches in advance. After updating, restart PHP-FPM, Apache modules and all long-running PHP processes such as queue workers and schedulers; these continue running the old binary until restarted. Container images must be rebuilt and redeployed with the patched PHP version. Confirm the fix through package changelogs or vendor advisories rather than version strings, since distributions often backport fixes without changing the upstream version number.

What should I do if I can't patch PHP2Shell immediately?

PHP’s official position is that only a full update is a complete solution. Interim measures that reduce exposure include: rejecting requests whose Content-Type contains multipart/form-data at the web server before they reach PHP (covering all HTTP methods, not just POST); setting memory_limit=-1 to remove the controllable OOM trigger for CVE-2026-109618; and setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 for CVE-2026-109619. For systems running PHP 8.1 or earlier that cannot be patched or compiled from PHP’s source-backports, the recommended action is isolation from public networks or taking them offline.

How do I detect PHP2Shell exploitation on my servers?

As of October 21, 2026, no vendor-published indicators of compromise exist yet, so detection relies on behavioral hunting. Look for PHP worker processes spawning shells or download utilities, unexplained worker crashes or segmentation faults in PHP-FPM and web server logs, unusual multipart/form-data requests (especially to endpoints that don’t accept uploads) from October 20, 2026 onward, new or modified files in web roots and upload directories, changes to .user.ini files or auto_prepend_file settings and new persistence indicators such as cron entries, SSH authorized_keys additions or unexpected outbound connections. Preserve web server and PHP logs from October 20 onward before patching or redeploying.

Protecting Against AiTM Attacks: Is Your Microsoft Environment at Risk?

October 21, 2026

Nick Schmitz

BLOG

5 min.

The identity threat landscape has shifted considerably over the past few years. Attackers have steadily moved toward more sophisticated techniques and Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing is near the top of that list. Microsoft observed a 146% rise in AiTM attacks in 2024 and the trend has continued into 2026.

TL;DR – If your Microsoft 365 environment relies on traditional multifactor authentication (MFA) without phishing-resistant authentication and or layered Conditional Access policies, AiTM attacks can bypass your defenses and hijack active sessions in real time.

Key Takeaways:

AiTM phishing has been commoditized through Phishing-as-a-Service platforms. AI-generated lures have eliminated the visual cues that users once relied on to identify phishing attempts.

Phishing-resistant authentication methods (FIDO2, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication) are the only category of MFA that AiTM proxies cannot relay, making them the most critical control to prioritize.

Deploying these controls in production environments with hybrid identity, legacy applications and third-party integrations requires deliberate sequencing and real-world risk assessment, not just baseline compliance.

A significant driver of AiTM growth is the Phishing-as-a-Service ecosystem. Platforms like Tycoon2FA have industrialized AiTM attacks. A threat actor with minimal technical skill can rent a fully functional proxy-based phishing kit, for as little as $120.

The result is a category of attack that was once the domain of sophisticated threat actors and is now widely accessible.

AI is accelerating this trend further. Phishing lures that used to be easy to spot, including awkward phrasing, odd formatting, generic greetings have all but vanished. Lures are increasingly generated by AI tools that produce polished, personalized and contextually convincing content at scale.

Research has found that AI-generated phishing attacks are becoming increasingly common. For organizations running Microsoft 365, this is a practical problem worth understanding.

What is AiTM and How Does It Work?

AiTM attacks build on the foundation of traditional man-in-the-middle tactics. This type of attack operates across multiple communication layers, from the network and transport layers all the way up to the application layer, relaying traffic in real time. Once positioned, the attacker actively intercepts the exchange between the victim and the legitimate service.

A user clicks a link in a phishing email and lands on an attacker-controlled reverse proxy. This proxy silently relays everything to the real login server.

The user enters their credentials and completes their multi-factor authentication (MFA) challenge, if applicable. To the user, everything looks normal, even the sign-in page will display their organization’s branding.

At the end of the authentication flow, once the server is satisfied, it issues a session cookie. The attacker’s proxy captures that token and injects it into their own browser.

They now hold a valid, active session and can navigate everywhere the user can. Traditional MFA methods like Short Message Service (SMS) codes and number matching cannot prevent this.

What Native Microsoft 365 Controls Can Help Address AiTM Risk?

Microsoft 365 includes several controls that directly address AiTM risk. The most effective are phishing-resistant authentication methods, specifically Fast Identity Online 2 (FIDO2) security keys, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication.

These methods are cryptographically bound to the legitimate domain, meaning a proxy cannot relay them. They are the only authentication methods that can stop AiTM if setup properly.

Beyond phishing-resistant authentication methods, Conditional Access is one of the most powerful tools available for reducing AiTM risk. Requiring compliant devices, restricting access to trusted locations and enforcing risk-based policies through Entra ID Protection creates a layered defense. An attacker would need to satisfy all of these conditions at once.

Even if a session cookie is stolen, with the proper setup these controls could stop that stolen session from being used.

These controls are well-designed and, when configured correctly, meaningfully reduce AiTM risk. The operational challenge for most organizations is getting from where they are today to a state where these controls are deployed, tuned and maintained without disrupting the business in the process.

Where to Focus Your Efforts to Reduce Risk

Microsoft 365 and Entra ID environments accumulate complexity quickly. Conditional Access policies layer on top of each other. Defender configurations drift from their original intent. Permissions granted for a specific project persist long after the project ends. Staying on top of it requires deliberate, recurring attention in three areas.

Start with Strategy

Passwordless authentication, Conditional Access architecture and zero trust roadmaps each touch identity, device trust, network segmentation and application access simultaneously. The challenge is rarely understanding what the target state looks like.

It’s sequencing the work across dependencies that already exist in production, with the budget and staffing currently available, without stalling the initiatives that are already in flight. Without a solid strategy serving as a foundation, you run the risk of introducing unintended gaps where an attacker can gain entry.

Assess Against Real-world Risk, Not Just Baselines

Recommended security baselines for Microsoft 365 and Entra ID are a reasonable starting point. The more valuable exercise is mapping your current configuration against attack patterns relevant to your organization. Looking at specific business email compromise (BEC) paths, token theft scenarios and lateral movement through overprivileged service principals will give you a greater understanding of where your AiTM risk lies.

Armed with this knowledge, you can make meaningful improvements that can significantly reduce the likelihood of a successful attack.

Account for Complexity in Policy Configuration and Deployment

Deploying security controls like Conditional Access, phishing-resistant MFA and Defender policies is straightforward in a clean environment. Most environments are not clean. Hybrid identity architectures, third-party integrations, legacy applications that do not support modern authentication and user experience considerations all introduce friction that turns a textbook deployment into something more nuanced.

Accounting for that complexity upfront prevents the cycle of deploying a control, breaking something, rolling it back and losing organizational trust in the process.

How GuidePoint Security Can Help

GuidePoint Security provides credentialed, expert cloud security services, including support across the Microsoft security stack. If you need help understanding where your Microsoft environment stands against AiTM and what it would take to close the gaps, we can help start that conversation.

FAQs

Can AiTM attacks bypass phishing-resistant MFA?

Not typically. FIDO2 security keys, passkeys and Windows Hello for Business are cryptographically bound to the legitimate domain. A proxy cannot relay that handshake, which is why these are the only MFA methods that stop AiTM.However, while AiTM cannot break the cryptographic exchange of true phishing-resistant MFA, attackers bypass these deployments using secondary techniques, including MFA Downgrade Attacks, Authorization-Layer Phishing and Post-Authentication Session Theft.

How do you detect an AiTM attack in progress?

Watch for sign-ins from unfamiliar locations or devices immediately after a legitimate authentication. Entra ID Protection can flag impossible travel, anomalous token activity and risk events that indicate session hijacking.

What should you do if a session token is stolen?

Revoke the compromised session immediately and force reauthentication for the affected account. Then investigate what the attacker accessed during the active session and reset any credentials or permissions that were exposed.

How do you deploy phishing-resistant MFA without disrupting the business?

Start with a pilot group and expand in phases based on role sensitivity and application compatibility. Legacy applications that do not support modern authentication need workarounds before you enforce phishing-resistant methods organization-wide.

GuidePoint Security announced Thursday it has promoted vendor partnerships leader Mark Thornberry to the role of chief business officer, as the cybersecurity powerhouse aims to accelerate its work with top AI platforms, hyperscalers and emerging startups, the solution provider told CRN exclusively.

In an interview with CRN, Thornberry said the promotion represents an expansion of the role he’s held for the past four years leading GuidePoint’s vendor relationships group. Expanded Role Builds on Thornberry’s Channel Leadership to Support GuidePoint’s Continued Growth

RESTON, Va., October 15, 2026 — GuidePoint Security, the cybersecurity advisor organizations rely on to protect what matters most, today announced the promotion of Mark Thornberry to Chief Business Officer (CBO). He previously served as Senior Vice President of Partnerships.Thornberry will continue to lead GuidePoint’s channel and strategic vendor partnerships while taking a broader role in company strategy and cross-functional growth. As CBO, he will oversee GuidePoint’s relationships with leading AI platforms to develop new opportunities for customers. He will also drive the company’s hyperscaler and cloud alliances, evaluate new routes to market and deepen relationships across the venture capital and private equity ecosystem to identify new technologies and expand GuidePoint’s contributions to the cybersecurity landscape.“Mark helped build the playbook for channel success at GuidePoint and has made partnerships a core part of how we serve customers,” said Scott Rachford, CEO of GuidePoint Security. “As Chief Business Officer, he will bring the market perspective, relationships and execution discipline behind that success to new areas of the business. He knows how to develop an opportunity, prove it works and bring the right teams together to scale it — exactly what we need to accelerate our next stage of growth.”Before joining GuidePoint Security in 2020, Thornberry spent more than a decade building and leading channel organizations at Cisco, Lacework, OpenDNS, WatchGuard Technologies and CDW.
